common_name: Shirley Primrose Chrysanthemum (Giant Primrose-Yellow Irregular Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Shirley Primrose is a giant-flowered irregular incurve exhibition type classed AA, the largest size designation in the NCS system.

directions: Shirley Primrose is an irregular-incurve exhibition chrysanthemum whose broad, smooth ray florets incurve in a loose, irregular manner to build an immense, fully double bloom in soft primrose yellow, with the lower florets often swirling outward to give a skirted effect at the base. As an AA-size cultivar it needs a long, cool, frost-free season (or protected finishing under glass) to reach full size, and it is always grown as a single disbudded stem: pinch once in late spring to set the bud, then remove every side bud so all the plant energy drives the one terminal flower, staking early since the finished bloom is heavy. Propagate from fresh basal cuttings off overwintered stock each year rather than relying on an old clump, and overwinter stock under cover in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse where winters are severe.

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Leicester is one of the National Chrysanthemum Society's own reference examples of the reflex class.

directions: Leicester is a large-flowered reflex exhibition mum in clean white, its narrow-to-broad florets gracefully overlapping and curving downward in regular ranks, like layered bird plumage, to form a bloom nearly equal in breadth and depth with a full, slightly flattened top. Pinch the young plant once in late spring to set bud sites, then disbud to a single terminal flower for maximum show size, staking the stem early since the finished bloom is heavy enough to topple an unsupported plant. Root fresh basal cuttings from stock each late winter rather than dividing an aging clump, and overwinter stock under cover in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse where winters are harsh.

common_name: Doreen Statham Chrysanthemum (Medium Red Reflex Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Doreen Statham is one of the NCS's own reference examples of the reflex class, classed as a medium (B) size bloom.

directions: Doreen Statham is a mid-season reflex exhibition chrysanthemum bearing medium-sized, densely overlapping red florets that curve downward in neat regular ranks to form a full, somewhat flattened globe. Grow it as a single disbudded stem for show-quality size, pinching once in late spring to set the bud and removing side buds as they appear, or leave some side buds for a smaller branching spray. Propagate fresh basal cuttings from stock plants each year, and overwinter stock under cover in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse in cold-winter climates.

common_name: George Couchman Chrysanthemum (Bronze Regular Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; George Couchman is one of the NCS's own reference examples of the regular incurve class.

directions: George Couchman is a regular-incurve exhibition chrysanthemum whose comparatively short, broad ray florets smoothly incurve on all sides to build a true globular bloom in warm bronze, equal in breadth and depth like a perfect ball. Disbud to a single terminal stem for exhibition-size blooms, pinching once in late spring to set the bud and staking early since the finished flower head is heavy. Root fresh basal cuttings from overwintered stock each late winter rather than relying on an old clump, since this class is traditionally maintained through annual propagation for best bloom form.

common_name: Moira Chrysanthemum (Purple Regular Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Moira is one of the NCS's own reference examples of the regular incurve class.

directions: Moira is a late-season regular-incurve exhibition chrysanthemum with smoothly incurving ray florets in rich purple-lavender that build a dense, true-globular bloom with the disk fully concealed. Grow it as a single disbudded stem, pinching once in late spring to set bud sites and removing every side bud so the plant channels its energy into one well-formed terminal flower, staking the stem early. Propagate fresh basal cuttings from stock plants each late winter, and overwinter stock under cover in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse where winters are harsh.

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Fireflash is one of the National Chrysanthemum Society's own reference examples of the decorative class.

directions: Fireflash is a decorative-class exhibition mum with vivid red florets that incurve toward the top of the bloom while the lower florets reflex outward, giving a flatter, fuller-bodied flower than the globular incurve and reflex classes, with the disk never showing. It can be grown either disbudded for a single large bloom or left with side buds for a branching spray of smaller flowers, and it is valued for the excellent substance and lasting quality typical of decorative-class cultivars. Fertilize every two weeks from midsummer until buds show color, stake as needed, and propagate from fresh basal cuttings each year rather than an aging clump.

common_name: Alexis Chrysanthemum (Pink Intermediate Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Alexis is the National Chrysanthemum Society's own reference example of the intermediate incurve class.

directions: Alexis is an intermediate-incurve exhibition mum in soft pink, a class whose florets are shorter than the regular incurves and arranged more loosely, so the bloom reads as full-centered and globular overall but with an open, slightly flattened or creased center that often shows a hint of the obverse floret color for a subtle bicolor effect. Disbud to a single terminal stem for exhibition size, pinching once in late spring and staking early since the finished bloom is heavy. Propagate fresh basal cuttings from overwintered stock each year, and divide or discard old clumps rather than relying on them for show-quality blooms.

common_name: Kelvin Mandarin Chrysanthemum (Bronze-Orange Pompon Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Kelvin Mandarin is one of the National Chrysanthemum Society's own reference examples of the pompon class.

directions: Kelvin Mandarin is a pompon-class exhibition chrysanthemum whose short, smooth, broad ray florets incurve in a tight, regular manner to form a firm, ball-shaped bloom in warm bronze-orange with excellent substance and no disk ever showing. It can be grown as a single disbudded stem for a larger show pompon or left to branch as a terminal spray of smaller, uniformly round blooms. Fertilize every two weeks from midsummer until buds show color, and propagate fresh basal cuttings from stock plants each year to keep bloom quality high.

common_name: Lavender Pixie Chrysanthemum (Pink-Lavender Pompon Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Lavender Pixie is one of the National Chrysanthemum Society's own reference examples of the pompon class, grown at a smaller (C) size than Kelvin Mandarin.

directions: Lavender Pixie is a small-flowered pompon chrysanthemum in soft pink-lavender, its short, smooth florets incurving tightly to form a firm, half-round button bloom under an inch to a few inches across, never showing a disk. Grown as a terminal spray rather than disbudded, it produces many uniform small pompons per stem, making it useful both for show spray classes and as a cut flower. Pinch stem tips through early summer to encourage a well-branched spray habit, and propagate fresh basal cuttings from stock each year.

common_name: By Jove Chrysanthemum (Red Single-Flowered Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; By Jove is grown and shown in the National Chrysanthemum Society's single/semi-double class.

directions: By Jove is a single-flowered exhibition chrysanthemum bearing one to several rows of broad, flat red ray florets arranged daisy-fashion around a prominent, flattened central disk, the classic uncomplicated bloom form that shows off both petal color and the contrasting disk floret color at once. Grow it as a single disbudded stem for the largest show-quality flower, or leave it to branch for a multi-bloom spray. Propagate fresh basal cuttings from overwintered stock each year, staking as needed since the open, daisy-form bloom sits atop an otherwise unsupported stem.

common_name: Prom Queen Chrysanthemum (Pink Anemone-Form Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Prom Queen is an early-flowering anemone-class exhibition cultivar.

directions: Prom Queen is an anemone-form exhibition chrysanthemum in pink, the class distinguished by a ring of flattened outer ray florets surrounding a tall, prominently raised cushion of elongated disk florets, giving each bloom a distinctive two-tiered, pincushion-like profile rather than a flat daisy face. It flowers early in the exhibition season, finishing ahead of most other disbud classes. Disbud to a single terminal stem for exhibition size, and propagate fresh basal cuttings from stock plants each year rather than relying on an aging clump.

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Vicksburg is a late-flowering spoon-class exhibition cultivar.

directions: Vicksburg is a spoon-type exhibition chrysanthemum in golden yellow, its elongated tubular florets radiating horizontally from a flat, prominent disk and opening only at the tip into a flattened, spatulate spoon shape, giving the bloom an airy, wheel-spoke appearance quite different from the dense, fully double classes. Disbud to a single terminal stem for show size, staking early since the open floret arrangement can be top-heavy once fully developed. Propagate fresh basal cuttings from overwintered stock each year to maintain bloom quality.

common_name: Bunker Hill Chrysanthemum (Yellow Quill-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Bunker Hill is a mid-season quill-class exhibition cultivar.

directions: Bunker Hill is a quill-type exhibition chrysanthemum in clear yellow, with elongated, straight tubular ray florets that stay closed or only slightly open at the tip, producing a fully double bloom with no disk ever visible and a bristly, radiating texture distinct from the open-tipped spoon class. Grow it as a single disbudded stem for exhibition-quality size, pinching once in late spring and staking the stem early since the dense quilled bloom is heavy. Propagate fresh basal cuttings from stock plants each year rather than dividing an old clump.

common_name: Fleur de Lis Chrysanthemum (Purple Spider-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Fleur de Lis is one of the National Chrysanthemum Society's own reference examples of the spider class.

directions: Fleur de Lis is a spider-type exhibition chrysanthemum in rich purple, its long, wiry tubular florets radiating outward in a wide variety of directions and terminating in distinctive coils or hooks rather than the straight points of the quill class, with no disk ever showing through the dense, feathery tangle of petals. Disbud to a single terminal stem for maximum bloom size, staking early and handling the finished flower carefully since the fine, curling florets are easily damaged. Propagate fresh basal cuttings from overwintered stock each year to maintain the delicate bloom form.

common_name: Wisp of Pink Chrysanthemum (Pink Brush-and-Thistle-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Wisp of Pink is one of the National Chrysanthemum Society's own reference examples of the brush-and-thistle class and is grown to a terminal spray rather than disbudded.

directions: Wisp of Pink belongs to the unusual brush-and-thistle class, its very fine, tubular pink ray florets somewhat flattened, twisted, and drooping in the thistle-like style, forming a loose, airy cluster of small blooms quite unlike any of the fully double classes. It is grown as a branching terminal spray rather than disbudded, producing numerous small, textured flowers per stem that read as a soft haze of color rather than individual blooms. Pinch stem tips through early summer to build a well-branched spray habit, and propagate fresh basal cuttings from stock each year.

common_name: Satin Ribbon Chrysanthemum (Pink Unclassified/Exotic-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Satin Ribbon is one of the National Chrysanthemum Society's own reference examples of Class 13, Unclassified (Exotic).

directions: Satin Ribbon is classed Unclassified (Exotic) because its pink ray florets combine traits of more than one standard class, broad, ribbon-like, and partly spatulate, twisting and swirling in an irregular pattern that does not fit neatly into the incurve, reflex, spoon, or quill definitions. Disbud to a single terminal stem to let the unusual twisted floret form develop to full size, staking early since the bloom can be top-heavy. Propagate fresh basal cuttings from overwintered stock each year, as this novelty class is maintained through annual propagation rather than left to an aging clump.
